blocks.text: A tailor in Aba measures your chest with a tape marked in centimetres and that is good enough for a shirt. But if a mechanic used the same tape to measure a piston he would ruin the engine, because a piston must be right to a hundredth of a millimetre. Choosing the instrument is part of doing the measurement correctly.

blocks.markdown:
Every instrument has a smallest division it can read, called its **least count** or **precision**. You cannot report a result finer than the instrument allows: a metre rule can never legitimately give you $12.437\ \text{cm}$.

So the first question in any practical is: *what precision does this measurement need?* Then pick the cheapest instrument that reaches it.

blocks.title: Least count
blocks.text: The smallest change in a quantity that an instrument can detect — the value of one division on its finest scale. A metre rule has a least count of 0.1 cm (1 mm); a vernier calliper 0.01 cm (0.1 mm); a micrometer screw gauge 0.01 mm.

blocks.markdown:
### Reading a vernier calliper

A vernier calliper has a fixed **main scale** graduated in millimetres and a sliding **vernier scale** with 10 divisions that together span only 9 mm. Each vernier division is therefore $0.9\ \text{mm}$, and the difference between one main division and one vernier division is $0.1\ \text{mm} = 0.01\ \text{cm}$. That difference is the least count.

To read it:

1. Read the main scale just **before** the vernier zero mark.
2. Find the vernier division that lines up exactly with any main-scale mark.
3. Multiply that division number by the least count and add it on.

blocks.title: Reading a vernier calliper
blocks.prompt: On a vernier calliper the zero of the vernier scale lies just past the 3.2 cm mark on the main scale, and the 4th vernier division coincides with a main-scale mark. What is the reading?

steps.text: Main scale reading: the last main-scale mark passed by the vernier zero.
Vernier scale reading: the coinciding division number multiplied by the least count of 0.01 cm.
Quote the answer to two decimal places, matching the precision of the instrument.

blocks.markdown:
### Reading a micrometer screw gauge

The micrometer has a **sleeve (main) scale** graduated in millimetres with half-millimetre marks below the line, and a rotating **thimble** with 50 divisions. One full turn of the thimble advances the spindle by $0.5\ \text{mm}$, so one thimble division is $\frac{0.5}{50} = 0.01\ \text{mm}$.

Reading $=$ sleeve reading (including any half-millimetre mark) $+$ thimble division $\times\ 0.01\ \text{mm}$.

blocks.title: Reading a micrometer screw gauge
blocks.prompt: The sleeve of a micrometer shows 5.5 mm and the thimble reads 32 divisions. Find the diameter of the wire being measured.

steps.text: Sleeve reading, remembering the half-millimetre mark is exposed.
Thimble reading: one division is 0.01 mm.
State the final value with its unit.

blocks.title: Zero error
blocks.text: Close the jaws before you measure. If the instrument does not read exactly zero it has a zero error. A positive zero error (reads +0.03 mm when closed) must be SUBTRACTED from every reading; a negative zero error must be ADDED. Skipping this check makes every result in your table wrong by the same amount.

items: Check and record the zero error before taking any readings.
Look at the scale straight on to avoid parallax error.
Tighten a micrometer using the ratchet, not the thimble, so you do not crush the object.
Read a measuring cylinder at the bottom of the meniscus, with your eye level with it.
Repeat each reading and take the mean to reduce random error.

blocks.title: WAEC practical tip
blocks.text: When timing oscillations, never time just one. Time 20 oscillations and divide by 20. Your reaction time of about 0.2 s is a much smaller fraction of 40 s than of 2 s, so the percentage error in the period drops twentyfold.

points: Least count is the smallest division an instrument can read; never quote a result finer than that.
Metre rule: 0.1 cm. Vernier calliper: 0.01 cm. Micrometer screw gauge: 0.01 mm.
Vernier reading = main scale reading + (coinciding division × 0.01 cm).
Micrometer reading = sleeve reading + (thimble division × 0.01 mm).
Subtract a positive zero error and add a negative one, and always read scales square-on to avoid parallax.
